          "exact_quote": "As $B\\to\\infty$, with $b=b(B)$ and $m_*$ defined above, $$\\begin{aligned}\n b(B)&=\\frac B2+\\frac{\\log(4\\pi B)+1}{\\pi}+o(1),\\\\\n m_*&\\sim\\frac{8}{\\pi e\\sqrt B}\\,e^{-\\pi B/2},\\\\\n 2\\int_{-B}^B\\rho_B(x)\\,dx\n       &=\\frac{B^2}{4}+\\frac B\\pi\\log B+O(B).\n \\end{aligned}\n \\label{eq:B5}$$ There are positive constants $c_1,C_1$ such that, for all sufficiently large $B$, $\\rho_B\\ge c_1\\sqrt B$ within distance one of either endpoint, and $\\rho_B\\le C_1B$ throughout the interval.           "anchor": "stmt-lem-bethe-algebra",
          "exact_quote": "Suppose the momenta and auxiliary variables are nonsingular solutions of $$\\label{eq:B8}\n \\begin{aligned}\n e^{ik_j\\mathcal W}\n   &=e^{i\\zeta+2i\\chi}\n       \\prod_{t\\ne j}\\frac{k_j-k_t+2i}{k_j-k_t-2i}\n       \\left(\\frac{Q_0(k_j-i)}{Q_0(k_j+i)}\\right)^2,\n       &&1\\leq j\\leq n_p,\\\\\n e^{-2i\\chi}\\prod_{j=1}^{n_p}\n       \\frac{a_r-k_j-i}{a_r-k_j+i}\n   &=\\prod_{s\\ne r}\\frac{a_r-a_s-2i}{a_r-a_s+2i},\n       &&1\\leq r\\leq M.\n \\end{aligned}$$ Here nonsingular means that the displayed rational functions and the coefficient formulas in the proof are defined by ordinary substitution. For each binary index, apply the upper-right entries $B(a_1),\\ldots,B(a_M)$ of the spin-$\\frac12$ monodromy defined below to the all-up vector. The tensor product of these two vectors, propagated by <a href=\"#eq:bethe-R\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq:bethe-R\">[eq:bethe-R]</a>, gives a periodic twisted eigenfunction of $H_2$ whenever it is nonzero. Its energy is $\\sum_j k_j^2$.*\n\n\n*More generally, let $S_J$ be the spin-$J$ angular momentum matrices, $g_J$ the spin-$J$ representation of $g$, $\\sigma$ the Pauli matrices, and $$\\mathcal L_J(x)=x-2iS_J\\cdot\\sigma,\n \\qquad F(u)=\\prod_{j=1}^{n_p}(u-k_j).$$ In the product of $\\mathcal L_J(u-k_j)$, put later physical sites on the left. Its auxiliary trace with twist $g_J^{-1}$ has eigenvalue $$\\label{eq:B9}\n t_J(u)=\\sum_{m=-J}^{J}e^{-2im\\chi}F(u-2im)\n \\frac{Q_0(u-i(2J+1))Q_0(u+i(2J+1))}\n      {Q_0(u-i(2m+1))Q_0(u-i(2m-1))}.$$ All these identities continue meromorphically in the variables. A nonzero continuation limit of the plane eigenfunction is again an eigenfunction at the limiting parameters.",

          "anchor": "stmt-lem-bethe-line",
          "exact_quote": "For every fixed integer $n_p=2M+\\ell\\geq0$, every $c>0$, and every $s>0$, the heat kernel of $H_c$ on the ordered line chamber is $$\\begin{split}\n e^{-sH_c}(X,Y)\n  ={}&\\sum_{\\ell'+2m'=n_p}\n       \\frac{(2c)^{m'}}{\\ell'!\\,m'!}\n       \\int_{\\mathbb R^{\\ell'+m'}}\n       E_X^{\\ell'm'}(k,u)E_Y^{\\ell'm'}(k,u)^\\dagger\\\\\n    &\\quad{}\\times\n       \\exp\\left\\{-s\\left(\n           \\sum_{a=1}^{\\ell'}k_a^2+\n           2\\sum_{a=1}^{m'}u_a^2-\\frac{m'c^2}{2}\n                    \\right)\\right\\}\n       \\prod_{a=1}^{\\ell'}\\frac{dk_a}{2\\pi}\n       \\prod_{a=1}^{m'}\\frac{du_a}{2\\pi}.\n\\end{split}\n\\label{eq:B10}$$ Empty products and the vacuum term have their usual value $1$. The transform defined by the kernels in <a href=\"#eq:B10\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq:B10\">[eq:B10]</a>, with the square roots of the displayed weights, is an isometry. Moreover, $H_c+Mc^2/2\\geq0$, and its quadratic form is the integral of $$\\sum_{a=1}^{\\ell'}k_a^2+\n  2\\sum_{a=1}^{m'}u_a^2+\\frac{(M-m')c^2}{2}$$ against the squared modulus of this transform.",

          "exact_quote": "Under the parameter assumptions at the start of this Section, for every $\\mathcal W\\geq W$, <a href=\"#eq:B13\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq:B13\">[eq:B13]</a> has a reflection-symmetric solution with $v=0$ and $u_1<\\cdots<u_M$. Define $$Z_c(x)=\\frac{x}{\\pi}\n    +\\frac{1}{\\pi\\mathcal W}\\sum_{j=1}^M\n           \\arctan\\frac{x-u_j}{4}\n    -\\frac{\\ell}{2\\pi\\mathcal W}\\varphi(x),\n \\qquad d(x)=Z_c'(x).$$ Then $Z_c$ is odd and $$d(x)=\\frac1\\pi+\\frac1{\\mathcal W}\\sum_jK(x-u_j)\n             -\\frac\\ell{\\mathcal W}(K_1-K_3)(x),\n \\qquad\n Z_c(u_j)=\\frac{j-(M+1)/2}{\\mathcal W}.$$ Let $B_c>0$ be determined by $Z_c(B_c)=M/(2\\mathcal W)$. At $\\mathcal W=W$ one also has $B_c\\geq B_*-O(1)$.*\n\n4.  *The full Jacobian of <a href=\"#eq:B13\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq:B13\">[eq:B13]</a>, including the single equation when present, is invertible.       "evidence": [

          "anchor": "stmt-lem-rg-free",
          "exact_quote": "For either initial precision and either admissible shape, the free block iteration has uniformly elliptic, exponentially localized precisions $K_h$, conditional means $\\mathsf P_h$, conditional covariances $C_h$, and positive edge stacks. Constants needed to choose $L$ are independent of sufficiently large $L$.*\n\n\n*For a Brownian strip the edge lift consists of the horizontal term $l^{-1}$ and a positive matrix on the two endpoint values of each vertical edge. If $z$ is the vertical edge Laplacian symbol, this matrix is $$B_l(z)=l\\sum_{m\\ge1}J_m^*\n          \\bigl(1+l^2z/(\\pi m)^2\\bigr)^{-1}J_m,\n \\qquad J_s(c,c')=(1-s)c+sc',\n \\label{eq:R3}$$ where $J_m$ is the $m$th normalized sine coefficient of $J_s$. It is analytic near $[0,4]$, with uniform positive lower and upper bounds on that real interval. The formula holds also for cut vertical arrays, using their existing bonds. The affine precision, after strips are summed, is $\\operatorname{diag}(l^{-1},l)$.",

        }

        {
          "anchor": "stmt-lem-rg-observation",
          "exact_quote": "For neighboring blocks $Y,Y'$ and their coarse edge $E$, $$r'_E\\le\\frac C L\\sum_{e\\subset Y\\cup Y'}r_e\n       +C\\bigl(|\\eta_Y|+|\\eta_{Y'}|\\bigr),\n \\label{eq:R8}$$ where $\\eta$ denotes the observation displacement, with its real coordinate measured before reduction.           "anchor": "stmt-lem-rg-joint",
          "exact_quote": "Fix a primary pattern and the complete-support convention above. Form local factors from: nonlinear rows minus their affine squares; stationary squares; old polynomial and regular-error terms; exceptional numerical defects; determinant and Gaussian-ratio chains; Haar Jacobian ratios; opened default-profile failures; and old covering weights. Include the compulsory cores and their frozen integrations.*\n\n*Suppose their ordinary smooth factors have envelopes $C_Lg^r\\operatorname{poly}(M_j,p_j,s)$ of positive order $r$; ratio exponents have bounds $$|Q_\\alpha(Z)|\\le e_\\alpha\n        \\left(1+\\sum_{x\\in I_\\alpha}|Z_x|^2\\right);$$ their eighth-root support-hit sums are sufficiently small; and every selection of $n$ distinct failure tests has simultaneous probability at most $\\exp(-c_Lp_j^2n/M_j^D)$. Suppose further that the frozen integral of each core satisfies $$\\int|B_c|\\le\\exp\\{-c_Lp_j^2s_c+\n C_LM_j^D(1+|\\log g|)s_c\\}$$ uniformly in the Gaussian arguments, while retaining the output-flag and curvature reserves. Here $B_c$ is the core integrand; its integral includes the frozen quaternion and real variables and the residual integer and tag sums, with Gaussian and output arguments held fixed. Suppose also that differentiation through hard dependencies can be represented by one simultaneous transport whose fixed-order $L^4$ scores cost a polynomial in total load and a fixed power of $g^{-1}$. Whenever such a negative power occurs, retain a core, failure, or exponentially accurate factor to pay it. Assume explicitly that every allowed differentiated product is a sum of polynomially many terms retaining the ordinary and ratio envelopes and the closed failure supports, apart from these score factors; a marked discrepancy uses its replacement envelope.*\n\n*Then every finite selection has a joint integral bound equal to the product of its stated majorants times a fixed polynomial in total load. This holds through eight normalized output derivatives for empty output inventory, and through seven derivatives for one marked input or parameter discrepancy. With nonempty output inventory it gives the sup norm and the corresponding discrepancy bound. A core with $s_c$ seeds retains $e^{-c_Lp_j^2s_c}$ after fixed losses, and each failure test retains $e^{-c_Lp_j^2/M_j^D}$; ratio chains may use their eighth-root envelopes. Disjoint complete supports factor exactly; overlapping factors require no independence.",
          "source_id": "PM-215.3"
        }

          "anchor": "stmt-lem-rg-canonical",

          "anchor": "stmt-thm-rg-step",
          "exact_quote": "Choose the constants in the order specified at the end of this section. For every sufficiently large $H$, every admitted layer $j\\ge1$, every admitted rectangle or bulk density of Definition <a href=\"#def:rg-retained-class\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"def:rg-retained-class\">30</a>, and either seam, the normalized block observation of Lemma <a href=\"#lem:rg-observation\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"lem:rg-observation\">31</a> has an exact output in the same class, provided the output kinetic coefficients remain in the next admitted bands. In input normalization for the $w$ coefficients, each of the four kinetic coefficients changes by $$\\alpha+\\kappa/B+O_L(H_j^{-1.05}),\n \\label{eq:R6}$$ where the direction and field indices are understood. The bounded coefficients $\\alpha,\\kappa$ and the next polynomial coefficients are given by the full-kernel Taylor map constructed below.*\n\n\n\n\n*For a Brownian input and a flat reference input on common lists, their outputs satisfy, for fixed $q_*<1$ and $c>0$, $$\\begin{split}\n U'&\\le q_*U+C_LL^{-h}+C_LH_j^{-c}|\\lambda|,\\\\\n |\\lambda'-\\lambda|&\\le C_LU+C_LL^{-h}\n                                      +C_LH_j^{-c}|\\lambda|.\n \\end{split}\n \\label{eq:R7}$$ The coefficients in $\\lambda'$ use output units, so the second estimate includes the real-coordinate conversion by $T$. No discrepancy of the old phase parameter is required. The restricted curvature cap renews with $$F_{h+1}=F_h+c_L\\sqrt\\beta\\,p_j.\n \\label{eq:R10}$$ Per output site, after the incoming scalar has been propagated, the scalar increment is $$4(L^2-1)\\log g+V_L(l_q,l_w,\\chi,T,h)+O_L(H_j^{-1}),\n \\label{eq:R11}$$ where $V_L$ is real, uniformly bounded and Lipschitz on the admitted bands.           "exact_quote": "The quantity <a href=\"#eq:init-rough-size\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq:init-rough-size\">[eq:init-rough-size]</a> controls a $\\nu$-Hölder rough-path norm, and $$\\Pr\\{\\mathcal N>D\\}\\le C e^{-cD^2}.$$ The same bound holds for a Gaussian bridge. Adding a path with bounded first derivative, or applying a smooth deterministic orthogonal rotation to the driving increments, preserves these estimates with the corresponding deterministic norm costs. Its total density obeys $$\\begin{aligned}\n K(1)&\\le Cg^{-4}\\exp(-cg^{-2}r_{e_x}^2),\n \\label{eq:init-heat-bound}\\\\\n K(1_{\\{\\mathcal N>D\\}})&\\le Cg^{-4}e^{-cD^2},\n \\label{eq:init-conditioned-tail}\n\\end{aligned}$$ uniformly in the endpoints. There exists $0<\\vartheta<1$ such that, for every set $I$ of unoriented rows and either time seam, $$\\frac{1}{Z_{F,+}^{\\rm end}}\n \\int_{\\mathcal F}e^{X_F^\\eta}\\Xi_F^\\eta\n       \\exp\\left(\\vartheta\\sum_{e\\in I}Y_e\\right)d\\nu\n \\le \\exp(C_L|I|B_T^2\\log H).\n \\label{eq:R16}$$ The choices may make $1-\\vartheta$ smaller than any prescribed fixed inverse power of $\\log H$.",

          "anchor": "stmt-lem-comparison-flat-edits",
          "exact_quote": "The constants $\\varepsilon>0$ and $C$ can be fixed, in that order, so that the following holds for every sufficiently large $H$ and every admitted rectangle with both periods sufficiently large depending on $H$. For every flat configuration and every selected family of its regions $E_C$, there is a measurable probability distribution of flat replacement configurations that leaves all other sites unchanged, changes only integers incident on replaced sites, removes exactly the inventories of the selected regions, and creates no flagged bond.*\n\n\n*If $E$ is the union of the selected regions and $n=|E|$, there is a set $I_E$ of rows, containing every changed kinetic stencil, such that $|I_E|\\le C d^2n$.       "evidence": [
        {

<a id="pm-s4"></a>
## 4. Engineering Triptych

### Panel 1 - epistemic contract

- **invariant-microscopic-normalization**: The mass asymptotic uses normalized sphere measure, single-counted nearest-neighbor bonds, and the original lattice time step. Changing these conventions requires a new normalization calculation.
- **invariant-full-observable-gap**: The spin correlation detects the full transfer gap, including local rotation-invariant observables. The centered even sector has the stronger transfer norm bound stated in the sector comparison.
- **invariant-parity-width-and-density**: The Brownian parity asymptotic requires both the prescribed growing circumference and a density bound for every particle number attaining either parity maximum.
- **invariant-exact-terminal-matching**: The terminal affine discrepancy vanishes exactly. This equality makes the unbounded direct kinetic terms agree before integration of the remaining bounded discrepancies.
- **invariant-helicity-order-of-limits**: Helicity matching first takes the low-temperature limit at fixed volume and blocking depth, then increases the blocking depth, and finally increases the remaining period.
- **invariant-positive-trace-doubling**: Trace doubling bounds the logarithmic discrepancy between a positive operator trace and the corresponding power of its norm. The direct-sum extension requires a finite total trace.

### Panel 2 - negative knowledge

- **anti-finite-temperature-exactness**: Treat the leading mass asymptotic as an exact finite-temperature prediction with a certified numerical error. -> The limit does not supply a finite-coupling remainder bound or a numerical threshold for prescribed accuracy.
- **anti-transfer-prefactor-between-actions**: Reuse the prefactor after changing the microscopic interaction or lattice geometry. -> The normalization-sensitive finite coupling shift has only been established for the specified nearest-neighbor square-lattice model.
- **anti-ignore-maximizing-sectors**: Apply the Brownian parity formula after checking only a convenient particle sector. -> An unchecked maximizing sector may fall outside the band covered by the uniform spectral estimates.
- **anti-differentiate-partition-error**: Obtain the helicity comparison by differentiating the partition-function error estimate. -> A bound on partition values alone does not provide the twist-derivative control used to determine the finite coupling shift.
- **anti-positive-complex-density**: Treat the Brownian retained density or a restricted covering sum as a positive probability density and divide by it pointwise. -> Complex weights and signed restricted sums invalidate that relative comparison.
- **anti-arbitrary-operator-trace-bound**: Apply the trace-doubling inequality to an operator without positivity or without the required trace-class power. -> The argument relies on nonnegative normalized eigenvalues and finite trace sums.

### Panel 3 - reference implementation and oracle

Applicability: `not_applicable`. The engineering target is an asymptotic assertion about the full infinite-volume transfer gap, requiring analytic control of growing circles, regulator matching and successive limits. The source explicitly states: “The mass in our theorem is the gap of the full transfer operator obtained from local observables.” Its matching construction also uses a topological existence argument: “A map of nonzero boundary degree cannot extend over the ball, a contradiction.” A finite spectral check of the trace-doubling lemma would cover only an auxiliary inequality and would not certify this mass asymptotic or construct matched parameters with certified finite-coupling errors.

## 6. Applicability limits and search

- **limit-microscopic-model-normalization** (hypothesis): The exact mass prefactor belongs to the specified nearest-neighbor square-lattice interaction with probability sphere measure and single-counted bonds. Blocked use: ['Transplant the prefactor to another lattice geometry or microscopic action without repeating the normalization calculation.']
- **limit-asymptotic-without-finite-error** (approximation): The main mass formula determines a low-temperature limit. A certified relative error or an explicit accuracy threshold at a prescribed finite coupling is ABSENT. Blocked use: ['Use the leading asymptotic as an exact finite-temperature acceptance threshold.']
- **limit-full-gap-and-time-unit** (formal_scope): The mass concerns the full local-observable transfer space and is measured in the original lattice time unit. Blocked use: ['Identify an unrelated restricted-sector eigenvalue or a gap measured in a blocked time unit with the stated lattice mass without proving the conversion.']
- **limit-finite-graph-ferromagnetic-law** (hypothesis): The finite-graph covariance comparison uses nonnegative couplings, no external field and no pinned boundary. Blocked use: ['Apply the component-sign and covariance estimates directly to a frustrated graph, an external-field measure or pinned boundary data.']
- **limit-total-parity-versus-component-parity** (edge_case): Evenness under total inversion does not imply evenness under each component reflection. The visibility estimate requires the specified component-odd symmetry of both row functions. Blocked use: ['Replace the component-reflection hypotheses in the visibility estimate by total inversion parity alone.']
- **limit-fixed-coupling-visibility** (hypothesis): The visibility constant is independent of circumference at fixed coupling. The plane-gap identification fixes a trajectory before sending its circumference to infinity. Blocked use: ['Assume the visibility constant is uniform in a simultaneous low-temperature and large-circumference limit.']
- **limit-imported-admitted-trajectories** (hypothesis): The cylinder rates depend on imported admitted trajectories, calibration, seed estimates and the reference-depth restriction. Admission is not a claim of uniqueness of the bare coupling. Blocked use: ['Use the uniform cylinder rate for an arbitrary uncalibrated blocking sequence.', 'Assume a unique bare coupling for prescribed depth and terminal coupling.']
- **limit-brownian-width-and-all-maximizers** (hypothesis): The Brownian parity asymptotic requires the prescribed growing circumference and a uniform density band for every particle number attaining either parity maximum. Blocked use: ['Invoke the parity asymptotic at an arbitrary fixed circumference.', 'Check a convenient particle sector while leaving other maximizing sectors uncontrolled.']
- **limit-ground-state-sign-and-weight** (hypothesis): The identification of a transfer norm with a contact ground-state eigenvalue uses the balanced fixed-weight sector and its fixed color sign convention. Blocked use: ['Identify an arbitrary contact eigenstate or an eigenstate in an unchecked weight sector with the full transfer norm.']
- **limit-selected-endpoint-and-exterior-extension** (hypothesis): The dressed-energy sign and odd-mass interpretation use the selected endpoint condition and the whole-line exterior extension. An arbitrary interval or an unselected coupling does not inherit those conclusions. Blocked use: ['Evaluate the odd cost using a truncated interior solution without its prescribed exterior continuation.', 'Use endpoint asymptotics without selecting the coupling through the boundary condition.']

<a id="pm-s7"></a>
## 7. Complete mathematical paper


For the nearest-neighbor $`O(4)`$ model on the square lattice at inverse temperature <i>β</i>, we prove the exact low-temperature asymptotic

$`\displaystyle m_{\mathrm{lat}}(\beta)\sim 32\exp(\pi/4-1/2)\sqrt\beta\,\exp(-\pi\beta) \qquad (\beta\to\infty).`$

Here the mass is the gap of the full Osterwalder–Schrader transfer operator, including rotation-invariant local-observable sectors, in units of one original lattice time step.

<a id="sec:introduction"></a>
### Introduction

The two-dimensional $O(4)$ model is a basic example in which a local, rotation-invariant interaction produces a correlation length that grows exponentially with the inverse temperature. Its mass scale is predicted by asymptotic freedom, while the numerical prefactor is sensitive to the normalization of the microscopic interaction. We determine that prefactor for the nearest-neighbor square-lattice model. The mass in our theorem is the gap of the full transfer operator obtained from local observables.

<a id="pm-h-3"></a>
#### The model and the result

<a id="eq:gibbs"></a>
For an even integer $L_0\geq4$, let $\Lambda_{L_0}=(\mathbb Z/L_0\mathbb Z)^2$. A spin configuration is a family $\sigma=(\sigma_x)_{x\in\Lambda_{L_0}}$ with $\sigma_x\in S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. Let $\omega_3$ be normalized surface measure on $S^3$. At inverse temperature $\beta>0$, the periodic Gibbs measure is $$\label{eq:gibbs}
 \,\mathrm d\mu_{\beta,L_0}(\sigma)
 =\frac{1}{Z_{\beta,L_0}}
   \exp\!\left\{\beta\sum_{\langle xy\rangle}
                    \sigma_x\cdot\sigma_y\right\}
   \prod_{x\in\Lambda_{L_0}}\,\mathrm d\omega_3(\sigma_x).$$ Each unoriented nearest-neighbor bond occurs once. We use the periodic infinite-volume limit $\mu_\beta$, whose existence and uniqueness as a periodic local weak limit are supplied by (**SharpO4?**, Corollary 1.2).

<a id="eq:mass-definition"></a>
Write $x=(t,x_1)$, with the first coordinate interpreted as time, and let $\Theta$ reflect $t$ to $-t$. For bounded local functions supported in $t\geq0$, reflection positivity gives the semidefinite form <a id="eq:os-form"></a>$$\label{eq:os-form}
 \langle F,G\rangle_{\mathrm{OS}}
   =\mathbb E_{\mu_\beta}\bigl[(\Theta\overline F)G\bigr].$$ The quotient by its null space, followed by completion, is the Osterwalder–Schrader Hilbert space $\mathcal H_\beta$; the reconstruction framework originates in (Osterwalder and Schrader 1973) <a id="pm-cite-1"></a>[[OsterwalderSchrader1973](#ref-OsterwalderSchrader1973)]. Denote the vector represented by the constant function by $\Omega_\beta$. Translation by one time step induces a positive self-adjoint contraction $T_\beta$, with $T_\beta\Omega_\beta=\Omega_\beta$. Define $$\label{eq:mass-definition}
 m_{\mathrm{lat}}(\beta)
   =-\log\left\|T_\beta\big|_{\Omega_\beta^\perp}\right\|.$$ Thus the unit of mass is one original lattice time step. The orthogonal complement in <a href="#eq:mass-definition" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:mass-definition">[eq:mass-definition]</a> contains every sector generated by local observables, including rotation-invariant observables.

<a id="stmt-thm-main"></a>
<div id="thm:main" class="theorem">

**Theorem 1**. *For the measures <a href="#eq:gibbs" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:gibbs">[eq:gibbs]</a>, the full transfer gap <a href="#eq:mass-definition" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:mass-definition">[eq:mass-definition]</a> satisfies <a id="eq:main-limit"></a>$$\label{eq:main-limit}
 \lim_{\beta\to\infty}
    \frac{\exp(\pi\beta)}{\sqrt\beta}\,m_{\mathrm{lat}}(\beta)
       =32\exp\!\left(\frac\pi4-\frac12\right).$$*

</div>

The sharp-order theorem of (**SharpO4?**, Theorem 1.1) gives positive constants $c,C$ such that <a id="eq:sharp-order-input"></a>$$\label{eq:sharp-order-input}
 c\sqrt\beta\,\exp(-\pi\beta)
   \leq m_{\mathrm{lat}}(\beta)
   \leq C\sqrt\beta\,\exp(-\pi\beta)$$ for sufficiently large $\beta$. It also supplies the admitted renormalization trajectories and finite-volume estimates used below. Theorem <a href="#thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:main">1</a> identifies the limit within these bounds. We state the particular imported results at their points of use, together with their normalizations. All comparisons with the auxiliary regulator are proved in this paper.

<a id="pm-h-4"></a>
#### Historical context

For two-dimensional systems with continuous spin symmetry, absence of spontaneous magnetization and decay of correlations are separate questions. The theorem of Mermin and Wagner (Mermin and Wagner 1966) <a id="pm-cite-2"></a>[[MerminWagner1966](#ref-MerminWagner1966)] established the first phenomenon for finite-range isotropic Heisenberg systems at positive temperature. The low-temperature analysis of nonlinear sigma models by Polyakov (Polyakov 1975) <a id="pm-cite-3"></a>[[Polyakov1975](#ref-Polyakov1975)] and by Brézin and Zinn-Justin (Brézin and Zinn-Justin 1976) <a id="pm-cite-4"></a>[[BrezinZinnJustin1976](#ref-BrezinZinnJustin1976)] identified the renormalization mechanism behind an exponentially large correlation length for $O(n)$ models with $n>2$. Determining the complete leading asymptotic requires information beyond the leading renormalization flow.

The exact-mass prediction developed through the integrable continuum theory. Hasenfratz, Maggiore and Niedermayer (Hasenfratz, Maggiore, and Niedermayer 1990) <a id="pm-cite-5"></a>[[HasenfratzMaggioreNiedermayer1990](#ref-HasenfratzMaggioreNiedermayer1990)] obtained exact ratios of the physical mass gap to the renormalization-group scale $\Lambda_{\overline{\mathrm{MS}}}$ for the $O(3)$ and $O(4)$ sigma models by matching Bethe-ansatz calculations with perturbation theory. Hasenfratz and Niedermayer (Hasenfratz and Niedermayer 1990) <a id="pm-cite-6"></a>[[HasenfratzNiedermayer1990](#ref-HasenfratzNiedermayer1990)] extended the calculation to $O(n)$, $n\geq3$, starting from the factorized scattering description. These results give $m/\Lambda_{\overline{\mathrm{MS}}}=\sqrt{32/(\pi e)}$ for $O(4)$ and explain the relation of the prefactor to the renormalization convention. Passing from that prediction to the full gap of a specified lattice transfer operator requires control of the regulator comparison and of the observable sector that detects the gap.

Rigorous approaches include Kupiainen’s large-component expansion and mass-gap result (Kupiainen 1980) <a id="pm-cite-7"></a>[[Kupiainen1980](#ref-Kupiainen1980)]. That large-component regime differs from the fixed-$O(4)$ limit considered here. Our proof uses the sharp lattice estimates of (**SharpO4?**) as its constructive starting point. Two further companion arguments are relevant. The parity comparison in (**O3Pole?**) provides a finite-graph template that we adapt to $S^3$, and the integrated comparison in (**O3Continuum?**) provides the reference-measure argument used at the end of the regulator comparison. We give the adaptations needed for the present model, including the extra circle coordinate, complex weights, and rectangles with growing aspect ratio. The exact mass formula is obtained directly from these lattice and auxiliary-model estimates.

<a id="pm-h-5"></a>
#### Proof strategy

The proof passes through partition functions because they accommodate both the full transfer operator and the auxiliary model. It has three main ingredients: a comparison of observable sectors, a spectral calculation for the auxiliary model, and a comparison of the two regulators.

First, we show that the spin two-point function detects the full transfer gap. On any finite ferromagnetic graph, the covariance of two even spin monomials is bounded by a constant times the square of the largest spin correlation between their supports. Odd monomials have a bound with the first power. The constants depend only on the monomial degrees. Positivity of transfer spectral measures and polynomial density then control every local observable sector. A bounded odd detector on finite cylinders gives the converse comparison needed to pass between cylinder eigenvalues and the plane gap. These estimates express $m_{\mathrm{lat}}$ as the decay rate of the ratio of odd to even traces on growing rectangles.

<a id="eq:overview-brownian"></a>
Second, we introduce a Brownian regulator. Its spins are loops in $U(2)=(U(1)\times SU(2))/\{\pm1\}$, with space a circle of circumference $W$ and time discrete. Expanding the time interaction gives positive transfer operators $T_{n_p}$ indexed by a particle number $n_p\geq0$. A minus-center time twist multiplies the $n_p$-sector by $(-1)^{n_p}$. For $\ell=0,1$, let $\tau_\ell=\max_{n_p\equiv\ell\ ({\rm mod}\ 2)}\|T_{n_p}\|$. The spectral calculation yields $$\label{eq:overview-brownian}
 \log\tau_0-\log\tau_1
       \sim 32\sqrt2\,\sqrt b\,\exp(-\pi b)$$ on an explicitly specified scale of large circles, provided the maximizing particle numbers have density $n_p/W=b^2+O(b)$. Here $b$ is the auxiliary coupling. The proof constructs the required finite-circle eigenstates, identifies them with positive ground states of a contact Hamiltonian, and controls the other rotor winding terms. A nearby-fugacity estimate subsequently verifies the particle-density condition.

<a id="eq:overview-shift"></a>
Third, we match the Brownian regulator to the Wilson model <a href="#eq:gibbs" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:gibbs">[eq:gibbs]</a> augmented by a circle field constructed from a real Gaussian lift and a sum over its two winding numbers. Each winding parity imposes the corresponding sign twist on the Wilson spins. The matching has two outputs. On growing rectangles it controls absolute differences of partition functions after removing bulk scalar factors. Although the Brownian density may be complex, this estimate is obtained by integration against the positive augmented Wilson measure. The error is small enough to resolve the exponentially small odd trace. Separately, the construction matches finite-order response coefficients in fixed-volume expansions. The response to a small rotational boundary twist, or helicity, determines the finite shift $$\label{eq:overview-shift}
 \beta-b=\frac14-\frac{1+\log2}{2\pi}+o(1).$$ To extract the mass, we combine periodic time boundary conditions with a boundary condition that changes the sign of every spin on crossing the time seam. Their partition half-sum and half-difference isolate the two parities. In the augmented Wilson model, the added circle field contributes a zero-winding Gaussian factor and winding corrections. The latter are negligible at the precision needed for the odd trace. The Gaussian factor cancels in the parity ratio, and its contribution to time doubling is of smaller order than the mass term. Comparing time lengths $t$ and $2t$ then passes from Brownian traces to the norms $\tau_0,\tau_1$. Thus the partition comparison transfers the mass, while the response comparison fixes its normalization. Together, <a href="#eq:overview-brownian" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:overview-brownian">[eq:overview-brownian]</a> and <a href="#eq:overview-shift" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:overview-shift">[eq:overview-shift]</a> give Theorem <a href="#thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:main">1</a>.

<figure id="fig:comparison">

<figcaption>The two outputs of regulator matching. The partition estimate is used on growing rectangles, while the response comparison is obtained from a fixed-volume expansion before the volume is increased. Both follow from the matched trajectories; the response comparison is not obtained by differentiating the partition error bound.</figcaption>
</figure>

<a id="pm-h-6"></a>
#### Organization and conventions

Sections <a href="#sec:sector" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:sector">2</a> and <a href="#sec:cylinders" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:cylinders">3</a> establish the full-gap comparison and its finite-volume form. Sections <a href="#sec:brownian" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:brownian">4</a> and <a href="#sec:integral" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:integral">5</a> construct the auxiliary regulator and solve the integral equations governing its mass scale. Section <a href="#sec:bethe" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:bethe">6</a> proves the finite-circle spectral formula. Section <a href="#sec:rg" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:rg">7</a> develops the exact renormalization comparison, and Sections <a href="#sec:initialization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:initialization">8</a> and <a href="#sec:comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:comparison">9</a> initialize the Brownian density, match its trajectory, and integrate the terminal comparison. Section <a href="#sec:renormalization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:renormalization">10</a> computes the finite coupling shift. Section <a href="#sec:assembly" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:assembly">11</a> completes the proof, including the required particle-number and error estimates.

Throughout, $c,C>0$ may change from line to line. Dependence on a fixed parameter is indicated when it matters. We use $f\asymp g$ for two-sided bounds by positive constants independent of the parameter tending to its limit, and $f\sim g$ when $f/g\to1$. The letter $L$ below denotes the fixed dyadic blocking factor, rather than the torus side $L_0$ used in <a href="#eq:gibbs" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:gibbs">[eq:gibbs]</a>. Particle number is written $n_p$; $N$ denotes renormalization depth. The two lattice coordinates are denoted by $t,x$ once rectangular volumes are introduced.

<a id="sec:sector"></a>
### Spin correlations and the full transfer spectrum

A partition function counts every transfer eigenvalue, whereas a spin two-point function sees only states created by a spin component. We first relate these two measurements. The key estimate is finite-dimensional: the covariance of two even spin monomials is quadratic in the largest component two-point function between their supports. The proof adapts the three-component argument of (**O3Pole?**), replacing its conditional Ising–rotator decomposition by two conditional rotators. We include the proof because its treatment of several spin components is essential for the full gap.

Here a monomial is a product of individual spin components with coefficient one. Its site list has one entry for each factor, including repetitions.

<a id="pm-h-8"></a>
#### Conditional rotators and correlation signs

<a id="eq:wilson-graph-law"></a>
Let $\mathcal G=(V,E)$ be a finite graph and give $q_x\in S^3$, $x\in V$, the probability law $$d\nu_J(q)=Z_J^{-1}
 \exp\left(\sum_{xy\in E}J_{xy}q_x\cdot q_y\right)
 \prod_{x\in V}d\omega_3(q_x),
 \qquad J_{xy}\ge0.
 \label{eq:wilson-graph-law}$$ There is no external field and no pinned boundary. We write $\mathbb E_J$ for this expectation.

<a id="eq:wilson-xy-ginibre"></a>
We recall the finite-system inequalities used below. For a zero-field ferromagnetic plane rotator with angles $\theta_x$, every two integer vectors $k,l$ indexed by $V$ satisfy $$\mathbb E\cos(k\cdot\theta)\ge0,\qquad
 \operatorname{Cov}\bigl(\cos(k\cdot\theta),
                         \cos(l\cdot\theta)\bigr)\ge0.
 \label{eq:wilson-xy-ginibre}$$ These are the plane-rotator inequalities of Ginibre (Ginibre 1970) <a id="pm-cite-8"></a>[[Ginibre1970](#ref-Ginibre1970)]. For clarity, the needed version has a short replica proof. Fourier expansion with nonnegative coefficients gives the first assertion. For the second, take independent copies $\theta,\theta'$ and substitute $\theta=\varphi+\psi$, $\theta'=\varphi-\psi$. This surjective homomorphism of product tori preserves Haar integration. Each observable difference becomes $-2\sin(k\cdot\varphi)\sin(k\cdot\psi)$, and the replicated weight is $$\exp\left(2\sum_{xy\in E}J_{xy}
       \cos(\varphi_x-\varphi_y)\cos(\psi_x-\psi_y)\right).$$ Expanding it expresses twice the covariance as a sum of squares of real integrals with nonnegative coefficients. Absolute convergence holds on the finite graph. Differentiating a cosine mean in a bond coupling consequently shows that the mean is nondecreasing in that coupling. We also use the zero-field Ising GKS inequalities (Kelly and Sherman 1968) <a id="pm-cite-9"></a>[[KellySherman1968](#ref-KellySherman1968)]: sign-monomial means and their covariances are nonnegative. These are precisely the finite-system ingredients of the conditional argument in (**SharpO4?**).

<a id="eq:wilson-two-planes"></a>
A law of real variables is *associated* if any two bounded coordinatewise increasing functions have nonnegative covariance. At every vertex write $$q_x=\bigl(\cos\alpha_x\cos\theta_x,\,
           \cos\alpha_x\sin\theta_x,\,
           \sin\alpha_x\cos\phi_x,\,
           \sin\alpha_x\sin\phi_x\bigr),
 \qquad 0\le\alpha_x\le\frac{\pi}{2}.
 \label{eq:wilson-two-planes}$$ The sphere prior is the product of the two uniform circle laws and $\sin(2\alpha_x)\,d\alpha_x$. Given $\alpha$, the two circle systems are independent and have couplings $$J^L_{xy}=J_{xy}\cos\alpha_x\cos\alpha_y,\qquad
 J^R_{xy}=J_{xy}\sin\alpha_x\sin\alpha_y.$$

<a id="stmt-lem-wilson-signs"></a>
<div id="lem:wilson-signs" class="lemma">

**Lemma 2** (Association and single-component signs). *The $\alpha$ marginal in <a href="#eq:wilson-two-planes" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-two-planes">[eq:wilson-two-planes]</a> is associated. For two even-degree monomials each using a single spin component, the covariance is nonnegative when their components agree and nonpositive when they differ. The same signs hold for the two components of a zero-field ferromagnetic plane rotator.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-wilson-signs"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-wilson-signs</summary>

*Proof.* The density of $\alpha$ relative to its product one-site prior is proportional to $Z_L(\alpha)Z_R(\alpha)$. For either factor, denote its bond observables by $O_e$ and its couplings by $J_e(\alpha)$. At two distinct vertices, $$\partial_x\partial_y\log Z
 =\sum_e\mathbb E(O_e)\,\partial_x\partial_yJ_e
 +\sum_{e,f}\operatorname{Cov}(O_e,O_f)
                  \partial_xJ_e\,\partial_yJ_f.$$ All first coupling derivatives in the left plane are nonpositive; all those in the right plane are nonnegative. A nonzero mixed derivative at distinct vertices occurs only at a bond’s endpoints and is nonnegative. The bond means and covariances are nonnegative by <a href="#eq:wilson-xy-ginibre" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-xy-ginibre">[eq:wilson-xy-ginibre]</a>. Thus the logarithmic density has nonnegative mixed derivatives. It satisfies the FKG lattice condition and hence is associated (Fortuin, Kasteleyn, and Ginibre 1971) <a id="pm-cite-10"></a>[[FortuinKasteleynGinibre1971](#ref-FortuinKasteleynGinibre1971)]. For this continuous array, restrict to compact subintervals of $(0,\pi/2)$, apply the finite-grid FKG inequality to approximating densities, and pass to the limit. Bounded increasing functions follow by approximation and the usual monotone-class extension. The endpoint restrictions can then be removed.

For the plane-rotator assertion, write its components as $(\varepsilon\cos\gamma,\varepsilon'\sin\gamma)$, $0\le\gamma\le\pi/2$. Given $\gamma$, the signs are independent ferromagnetic Ising systems. The same mixed-derivative calculation with GKS proves association of $\gamma$. Including amplitude factors, the first-component monomial mean is nonnegative and decreasing in $\gamma$, while the second-component mean is nonnegative and increasing. Conditional independence gives the nonpositive covariance for unlike components. For like components, the conditional covariance is nonnegative by GKS and the covariance of conditional means is nonnegative by association.

In <a href="#eq:wilson-two-planes" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-two-planes">[eq:wilson-two-planes]</a>, a component-one monomial has conditional mean equal to its cosine amplitudes times a nonnegative linear combination of cosine-character means. It is nonnegative and decreasing in $\alpha$. A component-four monomial has a nonnegative increasing conditional mean, by a fixed rotation of the right circle. Conditional independence gives the nonpositive covariance between these components. For like components, the conditional covariance is nonnegative by <a href="#eq:wilson-xy-ginibre" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-xy-ginibre">[eq:wilson-xy-ginibre]</a>; the conditional means have the same monotonicity. Component symmetry supplies the remaining choices of components. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-9"></a>
#### The covariance comparison

<a id="stmt-prop-wilson-covariance"></a>
<div id="prop:wilson-covariance" class="proposition">

<a id="eq:sector-cov"></a>
**Proposition 3** (Finite-graph sector comparison). *For the law <a href="#eq:wilson-graph-law" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-graph-law">[eq:wilson-graph-law]</a>, let $P,Q$ be spin monomials of positive degrees $r,s$ with site lists $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y$, and put $$G=\max_{x\in\mathcal X,\ y\in\mathcal Y}\mathbb E_J(q_x^1q_y^1).$$ Then $G\ge0$, and a constant $C_{r,s}$ depending only on the degrees satisfies $$|\operatorname{Cov}_J(P,Q)|\le C_{r,s}
 \begin{cases}
  G^2,&r,s\ \text{even},\\
  G,&r,s\ \text{odd},\\
  0,&r+s\ \text{odd}.
 \end{cases}
 \label{eq:sector-cov}$$ If either monomial is constant, its covariance is zero. The estimate is independent of the finite graph and its nonnegative couplings.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-wilson-covariance"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-wilson-covariance</summary>

*Proof.* We first control coefficients in the positive pairing expansion. This treats the odd case and several even cases. For the remaining case we must also control the covariance of conditional means.

<a id="eq:wilson-pairings"></a>
The uniform sphere moment tensor vanishes in odd degree, and in degree $2h$ it is $$\int_{S^3}q^{i_1}\cdots q^{i_{2h}}\,d\omega_3(q)
 =\frac{1}{4\cdot6\cdots(4+2h-2)}
   \sum_{\pi}\prod_{\{b,c\}\in\pi}\mathbf1_{\{i_b=i_c\}},$$ where the sum runs over pairings of labeled factors. Expand each bond exponential in powers of the dot product and apply the tensor identity at each site. Following the contracted bond lines pairs the external factors, and every closed line contributes four. Thus, for arbitrary assigned external components, $$\mathbb E_J\prod_{b=1}^{r+s}q_{x_b}^{i_b}
 =\sum_\pi d_\pi
       \prod_{\{b,c\}\in\pi}\mathbf1_{\{i_b=i_c\}},
 \qquad d_\pi\ge0.
 \label{eq:wilson-pairings}$$ The $d_\pi$ do not depend on the component assignment. Repeated sites cause no difficulty because the factors remain labeled. Absolute convergence justifies regrouping the expansion. In particular the component two-point functions are nonnegative.

A pair is *crossing* if it joins $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$. When $r,s$ are odd, every pairing crosses. Fix one crossing pair and assign component four to its endpoints and component one to all remaining endpoints. The resulting moment contains $d_\pi$ as a nonnegative summand. Conditional on $\alpha$, the remaining left-plane monomial has mean in $[0,1]$, including all amplitudes. Its removal bounds the moment by the chosen component-four pair mean. Hence $d_\pi\le G$. Both separate monomial means vanish in odd total degree, so summing the pairing coefficients proves the odd case.

<a id="eq:wilson-crossing"></a>
When $r,s$ are even, every crossing pairing has at least two crossing pairs. Assign component four to one, component two to another, and component one to the remaining endpoints. In the left plane, Lemma <a href="#lem:wilson-signs" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:wilson-signs">2</a> bounds the joint mean of the component-two pair and the component-one monomial by the product of their nonnegative means. The latter monomial mean and its amplitudes are at most one. The surviving component-two pair mean, including its amplitudes, is decreasing in $\alpha$, because $$\mathbb E(\sin\theta_x\sin\theta_y\mid\alpha)
 =\tfrac12\mathbb E(\cos(\theta_x-\theta_y)\mid\alpha).$$ This also holds when $x=y$. The component-four pair mean is increasing in $\alpha$. Association bounds their product expectation by the product of the full pair means, each at most $G$. Therefore $$d_\pi\le G^2
 \quad\text{for every crossing pairing of two even lists}.
 \label{eq:wilson-crossing}$$

For two single-component even monomials, compare equal and different choices of their components. The products of their means agree by symmetry. Their joint moments differ by exactly the crossing contributions in <a href="#eq:wilson-pairings" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-pairings">[eq:wilson-pairings]</a>. By Lemma <a href="#lem:wilson-signs" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:wilson-signs">2</a>, the two covariances have opposite weak signs, so each absolute covariance is at most this difference. Equation <a href="#eq:wilson-crossing" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-crossing">[eq:wilson-crossing]</a> proves the bound. The same reasoning applies to every pair of even sublists with the original value of $G$. If $P$ or $Q$ has odd degree in some component, its separate mean is zero and every compatible joint pairing crosses. This also follows from <a href="#eq:wilson-crossing" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-crossing">[eq:wilson-crossing]</a>.

It remains to consider monomials even in every component. We use single-component replacements, whose full covariances are already controlled, to bound both terms in the conditional covariance decomposition. Write $P=P_LP_R$ by its two planes and put $$b_{P,L}=\mathbb E(P_L\mid\alpha),\qquad
 b_{P,R}=\mathbb E(P_R\mid\alpha).$$ Let $P_L^*$ replace all its components by component one and $P_R^*$ replace all its components by component three. Denote their conditional means by $B_{P,L},B_{P,R}$ and use the corresponding notation for $Q$. Then $$|b_{P,L}|,|b_{P,R}|\le1,\qquad
 0\le B_{P,L},B_{P,R}\le1,$$ with $B_{P,L}$ decreasing and $B_{P,R}$ increasing in $\alpha$.

Factor the common amplitude $A_P(\alpha)$ from the left plane. Its Fourier expansion and the expansion after replacement are $$P_L=A_P(\alpha)\sum_k c_k\cos(k\cdot\theta),\qquad
 P_L^*=A_P(\alpha)\sum_k d_k\cos(k\cdot\theta),\qquad
 |c_k|\le d_k.$$ Each sine or cosine supplies two exponential terms of modulus $1/2$. Since the total number of sine factors is even, the original coefficients are real and invariant under $k\mapsto-k$. Replacement changes their phases to positive coefficients. Collecting equal frequencies preserves their domination, including for repeated sites. The same argument applies in the right plane. By <a href="#eq:wilson-xy-ginibre" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-xy-ginibre">[eq:wilson-xy-ginibre]</a>, <a id="eq:wilson-fourier-covariance"></a>$$|\operatorname{Cov}(P_L,Q_L\mid\alpha)|
 \le\operatorname{Cov}(P_L^*,Q_L^*\mid\alpha),
 \label{eq:wilson-fourier-covariance}$$ and likewise for $R$.

Conditional independence gives $$\begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Cov}(P,Q\mid\alpha)
 ={}&\operatorname{Cov}(P_L,Q_L\mid\alpha)
                    \mathbb E(P_RQ_R\mid\alpha)\\
 &+b_{P,L}b_{Q,L}\operatorname{Cov}(P_R,Q_R\mid\alpha).
\end{aligned}$$ The other factors have modulus at most one, so its averaged absolute value is at most $$\mathbb E\operatorname{Cov}(P_L^*,Q_L^*\mid\alpha)
 +\mathbb E\operatorname{Cov}(P_R^*,Q_R^*\mid\alpha).$$ Each term is at most its full single-component covariance: the omitted covariance of conditional means is nonnegative by association. Both terms have already been bounded by $C_{r,s}G^2$.

We still need the covariance of the conditional means. The Fourier comparison shows that $B_{P,L}\pm b_{P,L}$ are nonnegative combinations of cosine-character means multiplied by their common amplitude. Both are decreasing; likewise $B_{P,R}\pm b_{P,R}$ are increasing. For $\alpha\le\widetilde\alpha$ this gives $$|b_{P,L}(\widetilde\alpha)-b_{P,L}(\alpha)|
 \le B_{P,L}(\alpha)-B_{P,L}(\widetilde\alpha),$$ and the corresponding increasing bound for the right plane. The factors $b_{P,R},b_{P,L}$ in the conditional mean need not be monotone. Their changes are nevertheless bounded by those of the increasing $B_{P,R}$ and decreasing $B_{P,L}$. To combine these two controls, put $$Y_P=b_{P,R}b_{P,L},\qquad D_P=B_{P,R}-B_{P,L}.$$ Using the modulus bounds on the $b$ functions yields $$|Y_P(\widetilde\alpha)-Y_P(\alpha)|
 \le D_P(\widetilde\alpha)-D_P(\alpha).$$ Consequently $D_P+Y_P$ and $D_P-Y_P$ are increasing. Apply association to these functions and to $D_Q\pm Y_Q$. Adding the two matching-sign inequalities and the two opposite-sign inequalities proves <a id="eq:wilson-conditional-means"></a>$$|\operatorname{Cov}(Y_P,Y_Q)|
 \le\operatorname{Cov}(D_P,D_Q).
 \label{eq:wilson-conditional-means}$$ On expanding the right side, the two same-plane terms are bounded by their full single-component covariances, as above. The two opposite-plane terms are exactly full single-component covariances by conditional independence; they enter with minus signs. Each is bounded in absolute value by the estimate already proved on even sublists. Empty sublists give constants and zero covariances. The total-covariance identity now proves the even case.

Finally, global spin inversion makes the joint moment zero when $r+s$ is odd, and at least one separate mean is zero. This proves all cases of <a href="#eq:sector-cov" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:sector-cov">[eq:sector-cov]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-10"></a>
#### Consequences for the plane and finite cylinders

An observable is *even* or *odd* according to its parity under simultaneous inversion $q_x\mapsto-q_x$ at every site. A *component reflection* reverses one fixed component at every site and leaves the others unchanged. The same definitions apply on a row. Thus total inversion is the product of the four commuting component reflections; being even under total inversion does not require being even under each of them.

For the original Wilson law, we write $q=\sigma$ and $m(\beta)=m_{\mathrm{lat}}(\beta)$. Let $r_*(\beta)$ be the supremum of the support of the $T_\beta$-spectral measure of $[q_0^1]$ in the OS Hilbert space of Section <a href="#sec:introduction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:introduction">1</a>.

<a id="stmt-prop-wilson-full-gap"></a>
<div id="prop:wilson-full-gap" class="proposition">

<a id="eq:full-gap"></a>
**Proposition 4** (The spin field sees the full gap). *For every $\beta>0$, in the periodic plane state, $$m(\beta)=-\log r_*(\beta)
 =-\log\lim_{n\to\infty}
       \bigl(\mathbb E_{\mu_\beta}q_0^1q_{(n,0)}^1\bigr)^{1/n}.
 \label{eq:full-gap}$$ The transfer norm on the even subspace orthogonal to the vacuum is at most $r_*(\beta)^2$. Its gap is therefore at least $2m(\beta)$. The logarithms can be read in the extended sense; the imported upper bound below makes them finite throughout the large-$\beta$ regime.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-wilson-full-gap"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-wilson-full-gap</summary>

*Proof.* The finite-graph estimate passes to the periodic plane limit for fixed monomials. Spatial translations are unitary in the OS form and commute with $T_\beta$. Translated one-spin vectors have the same spectral support. Thus OS Cauchy–Schwarz gives $$0\le\mathbb E_{\mu_\beta}
       (q_{(0,x)}^1q_{(n,y)}^1)\le\tfrac14r_*^n$$ for arbitrary spatial sites $x,y$. The factor $1/4$ is their one-site reflection norm squared.

A reflected polynomial transfer autocorrelation is a finite sum of monomial covariances at temporal separation at least $n$. For an odd polynomial, <a href="#eq:sector-cov" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:sector-cov">[eq:sector-cov]</a> bounds it by $C_P r_*^n$; for a centered even polynomial it bounds it by $C_P r_*^{2n}$. The spectral measures are positive, so their supports lie in $[0,r_*]$ and $[0,r_*^2]$, respectively. Polynomials on a fixed finite spin product are dense in the $L^2$ space of its marginal law. Reflection invariance gives $\|[F]\|_{\mathrm{OS}}^2\le\mathbb E|F|^2$, so this approximation also holds in the OS seminorm. Centering and parity symmetrization preserve density. Bounded spectral projections extend the spectral bounds to the full subspaces. Since $[q_0^1]$ is centered, the full nonvacuum norm is exactly $r_*$. Finally, the $n$th root of a moment of a positive spectral measure tends to the supremum of its support. This proves <a href="#eq:full-gap" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:full-gap">[eq:full-gap]</a>. ◻

</details>

For even integers $n,\ell\ge4$, let $Z_\beta(n,\ell)$ denote the Wilson partition function on the rectangular torus with $n$ time sites and $\ell$ spatial sites, with the same single-counted bonds and probability spin measure as in Section <a href="#sec:introduction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:introduction">1</a>. For an even spatial circumference $\ell\ge4$, let $\mathscr X_\ell=(S^3)^\ell$ with product probability measure. Put $V_\ell(s)=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}s_i\cdot s_{i+1}$, periodically, and define the row transfer kernel <a id="eq:wilson-row-kernel"></a>$$K_{\beta,\ell}(s,s')
 =\exp\left[\frac{\beta}{2}V_\ell(s)
       +\beta\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}s_i\cdot s'_i
       +\frac{\beta}{2}V_\ell(s')\right].
 \label{eq:wilson-row-kernel}$$ It is compact, with a continuous strictly positive kernel and a simple top eigenvalue $\lambda_1$. The tensor-power expansion of $e^{\beta s\cdot s'}$ makes it positive semidefinite and trace class. Write $$U_{\beta,\ell}=K_{\beta,\ell}/\lambda_1,\qquad
 \Omega_{\beta,\ell}>0,\quad\|\Omega_{\beta,\ell}\|_2=1,\qquad
 \tau_{\beta,\ell}=\lambda_2/\lambda_1.$$ For $\beta>0$ the kernel is not rank one, as its cross ratios vary with the row configurations. Hence $0<\tau_{\beta,\ell}<1$. Closing time gives $Z_\beta(n,\ell)=\operatorname{Tr}K_{\beta,\ell}^{\,n}$. These are the conventions of (**SharpO4?**). Denote the infinite-time cylinder expectation by $\omega_{\beta,\ell}$.

<a id="stmt-lem-wilson-detector"></a>
<div id="lem:wilson-detector" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:wilson-detector-overlap"></a>
**Lemma 5** (An odd detector for the first cylinder excitation). *The restriction of $U_{\beta,\ell}$ to the centered even row subspace has norm at most $\tau_{\beta,\ell}^2$. There is a real row function $F$, with $|F|\le1$, odd under reflection of one spin component, such that $$\omega_{\beta,\ell}(F\,F\circ\vartheta_n)
 \ge\frac{\tau_{\beta,\ell}}{1+\tau_{\beta,\ell}}\,
                    \tau_{\beta,\ell}^{\,n},\qquad n\ge0,
 \label{eq:wilson-detector-overlap}$$ where $\vartheta_n$ translates by $n$ rows.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-wilson-detector"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-wilson-detector</summary>

*Proof.* The finite-graph estimate passes to the infinite-time cylinder by the row transfer representation. Component vectors $q_x^i\Omega$ are centered, so their correlations across $n$ rows are at most $\tau^n$, suppressing $\beta,\ell$. The even polynomial estimate therefore places the spectral support of every centered even polynomial vector in $[0,\tau^2]$. Polynomials are uniformly dense in continuous row functions, and the continuous positive $\Omega$ has a positive minimum. Thus polynomials times $\Omega$ are dense in row space, proving the even-sector norm bound.

Choose a real unit $\tau$-eigenfunction $v$. Since $\tau>\tau^2$, its eigenspace is odd under simultaneous inversion. The four component reflections commute with one another and with $U$, so $v$ can have definite parity under each; at least one is odd. Relabel it as component one. The modulus $|v|$ is even. With $b_0=\langle\Omega,|v|\rangle^2$, positivity of the kernel and the even-sector bound give $$\tau\le\langle|v|,U|v|\rangle
       \le b_0+(1-b_0)\tau^2,
 \qquad b_0\ge\frac{\tau}{1+\tau}.$$ Take $F=\operatorname{sgn}v$, equal to zero on its zero set. Its overlap with $v$ is $\langle v,F\Omega\rangle=\langle|v|,\Omega\rangle$. Keeping this contribution in the positive spectral expansion of its correlation proves <a href="#eq:wilson-detector-overlap" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-detector-overlap">[eq:wilson-detector-overlap]</a>. ◻

</details>

The detector can involve the entire row. We next recover a component correlation with a cost polynomial in the circumference.

<a id="stmt-lem-wilson-visibility"></a>
<div id="lem:wilson-visibility" class="lemma">

**Lemma 6** (Visibility through component correlations). *For fixed $\beta>0$ there is a finite constant $C_\beta$, independent of even $\ell\ge4$, such that bounded row functions $F,G$ of modulus at most one, both odd under reflection of component one, satisfy <a id="eq:wilson-visibility"></a>$$|\omega_{\beta,\ell}(F\,G\circ\vartheta_n)|
 \le C_\beta\sum_{x\in R_0,\ y\in R_n}
                      \omega_{\beta,\ell}(q_x^1q_y^1),
 \qquad n\ge1.
 \label{eq:wilson-visibility}$$ Here $R_0,R_n$ are the two rows of $\ell$ sites.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-wilson-visibility"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-wilson-visibility</summary>

*Proof.* On a finite torus, write $$q_i=(\varepsilon_i u_i,\sqrt{1-u_i^2}\,l_i),\qquad
 \varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\},\quad u_i\in[0,1],\quad l_i\in S^2.$$ The prior is a product: $\varepsilon_i$ is fair, $l_i$ is uniform, and $u_i$ has density proportional to $\sqrt{1-u_i^2}$. Given $u,l$, the signs are a ferromagnetic Ising model with coupling $\beta u_i u_j$. In its Edwards–Sokal representation (Edwards and Sokal 1988) <a id="pm-cite-11"></a>[[EdwardsSokal1988](#ref-EdwardsSokal1988)], an edge between equal signs is open with probability $1-e^{-2\beta u_i u_j}$, and an edge between different signs is closed. Given the edges, cluster signs are independent and fair. If no cluster joins the detector rows, flip all clusters touching the first row. This reverses $F$ and leaves $G$ unchanged. Its conditional product mean is therefore zero. The absolute detector correlation is bounded by the row-connection probability, and then by the sum of pair-connection probabilities.

<a id="eq:wilson-fk-pair"></a>
For a pair $x,y$ the joint spin–edge representation gives $$\mathbb E(q_x^1q_y^1)
 =\mathbb E[u_xu_y\mathbf1_{\{x\leftrightarrow y\}}].
 \label{eq:wilson-fk-pair}$$ Condition on all edges, directions $l$, and amplitudes other than $u_i$. After summing the signs, each closed incident edge has factor $e^{-J}$ and each open edge has factor $e^J-e^{-J}$, where $J=\beta u_i u_j$. The cluster multiplicity depends only on the fixed edges. Raising $u_i\in[0,1/4]$ to $u_i+1/4\in[1/4,1/2]$ increases every open factor. Closed-edge factors and perpendicular factors $$\exp\bigl(\beta\sqrt{1-u_i^2}\sqrt{1-u_j^2}\,l_i\cdot l_j\bigr)$$ change by bounded ratios depending only on $\beta$ and degree four. The amplitude prior is bounded above and below on these intervals. Comparing their integrals proves $$\mathbb P(u_i\ge1/4\mid\text{all other data})\ge c_\beta>0$$ uniformly in the volume. Applying this twice by the tower property gives $\mathbb E[u_xu_y\mid\text{edges},l]\ge c_\beta^2/16$. The connection event is edge-measurable, so <a href="#eq:wilson-fk-pair" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-fk-pair">[eq:wilson-fk-pair]</a> bounds its probability by $16c_\beta^{-2}\mathbb E(q_x^1q_y^1)$. Summing proves the finite-torus estimate.

At fixed circumference the transfer representation converges to the cylinder for all bounded Borel row insertions: separate the ground projection, use their bounded multiplication norms, and let the excited trace tail tend to zero. The estimate therefore passes to the cylinder, including the sign detector. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:cylinders"></a>
### Cylinder masses and a partition-function rate

We now express the plane mass as the decay rate of a volume-canceling combination of square partition functions. Trace estimates will be uniform over the admitted cutoff trajectories. In contrast, the visibility argument will be applied only after fixing one trajectory and sending the circumference to infinity.

<a id="pm-h-12"></a>
#### The imported Wilson trajectory bounds

Here is the precise input from (**SharpO4?**). Fix its sufficiently large dyadic blocking factor $L$ and auxiliary parameters, and then choose the terminal reference coupling $H$ sufficiently large for its construction and mass bounds. Put $$H_j=H+\frac{\log L}{\pi}j,\qquad I_H=[0.9H,1.1H].$$ An *admitted nearest-neighbor trajectory of depth $N$* is the exact $N$-step block integration of the nearest-neighbor Wilson law constructed in (**SharpO4?** and 7.1). At every remaining depth $j=N,\ldots,0$, its retained density satisfies the controlled-class bounds in that source and its kinetic coupling lies in $[H_j/2,2H_j]$. The kinetic coupling is the coefficient extracted from the quadratic energy of a slowly varying retained spin field. Its initial value is the bare coupling $\beta$ and its final value is denoted by $h$. No uniqueness of an admitted bare coupling with given $N,h$ is assumed. The trace argument will use only the numerical conclusions of the following imported proposition.

<a id="stmt-prop-wilson-input"></a>
<div id="prop:wilson-input" class="proposition">

<a id="eq:wilson-seed"></a>
<a id="eq:wilson-input-upper"></a>
**Proposition 7** (Wilson trajectory input). *For each $N\ge1$ and $h\in I_H$ there exists an admitted nearest-neighbor trajectory of depth $N$ ending at $h$. Every sufficiently large bare coupling occurs in at least one such trajectory. There are fixed integers $N_0,M_0>0$, with $M_0$ dyadic, such that every admitted trajectory with $N\ge N_0$, terminal coupling $h\in I_H$, bare coupling $\beta$, and spacing $a=L^{-N}$ obeys <a id="eq:wilson-calibration"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 4\log Z_\beta(M_0/a,M_0/a)
 -\log Z_\beta(2M_0/a,2M_0/a)&\le2^{-10},
 \label{eq:wilson-seed}\\
 m(\beta)/a&\le\log8,
 \label{eq:wilson-input-upper}\\
 N\log L&=\pi\beta-\tfrac12\log\beta+O_{L,H}(1).
 \label{eq:wilson-calibration}
\end{aligned}$$ In particular $a\asymp_{L,H}\sqrt\beta e^{-\pi\beta}$. The error bound and the two preceding inequalities are uniform over these trajectories. The periodic plane limit is unique and has a positive full OS gap for every fixed $\beta>0$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-wilson-input"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-wilson-input</summary>

*Source and applicability.* Admission and coverage are (**SharpO4?**, Proposition 7.1); calibration is its Proposition 6.2. The seed <a href="#eq:wilson-seed" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-seed">[eq:wilson-seed]</a> is the concluding estimate in the proof of its Theorem 9.2: the reference depth and then the dyadic $M_0$ are fixed before the final depth varies. The upper bound is its Proposition 10.2. Periodic-limit uniqueness and the all-temperature full gap are its Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2. The sphere probability convention, single counting of bonds, even periods, and site-reflection one-step transfer coincide with ours. In particular the cited gaps concern the full local OS space, including rotation-invariant observables. ◻

</details>

Fix one admitted trajectory with $N\ge N_0$ and $h\in I_H$ for the following definitions and suppress its parameters. Physical lengths $t,w$ always have $t/a,w/a$ even integers at least four. Write $$\mathcal Z(t,w)=Z_\beta(t/a,w/a),\qquad
 U(w)=U_{\beta,w/a},\qquad E(w)=-a^{-1}\log\tau_{\beta,w/a}.$$ Define $$\begin{aligned}
 p(t,w)&=2\log\mathcal Z(t,w)-\log\mathcal Z(2t,w),\\
 \Delta(w)&=4\log\mathcal Z(w,w)-\log\mathcal Z(2w,2w),\\
 s(t,w)&=\operatorname{Tr}U(w)^{t/a}-1.
\end{aligned}$$ The top-eigenvalue scalar cancels in $p$, and every area-proportional free-energy term cancels in $\Delta$.

<a id="stmt-prop-wilson-partition-rate"></a>
<div id="prop:wilson-partition-rate" class="proposition">

<a id="eq:wilson-cylinder-rate"></a>
<a id="eq:partition-rate"></a>
**Proposition 8** (Uniform cylinder and partition rates). *<span id="prop:cylinder-rate" label="prop:cylinder-rate"></span> For all admitted trajectories of Proposition <a href="#prop:wilson-input" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:wilson-input">7</a> with $N\ge N_0$ and terminal coupling $h\in I_H$, there are constants $C_H,w_H<\infty$, independent of the trajectory, such that every dyadic $w\ge w_H$ satisfies $$\left|E(w)-\frac{m(\beta)}a\right|\le C_Hw^{-1/4}
 \label{eq:wilson-cylinder-rate}$$ and $$\left|-\frac{\log\Delta(w)}w-\frac{m(\beta)}a\right|
       \le C_Hw^{-1/4}.
 \label{eq:partition-rate}$$*

</div>

We first obtain uniform convergence of a truncated cylinder rate from exact rectangle identities. We then identify its limit with the plane gap and remove the truncation.

<a id="pm-h-13"></a>
#### Trace tails and rectangle identities

<a id="eq:rectangle-identities"></a>
<a id="eq:wilson-trace-advance"></a>
The transfer eigenvalues give $$p(t,w)=2\log(1+s(t,w))-\log(1+s(2t,w)).$$ If $1=u_1\ge u_2\ge\cdots\ge0$ are the eigenvalues of $U(w)$, the normalized trace weights at time $t$ are $\eta_i=u_i^{t/a}/(1+s(t,w))$. Thus $e^{-p(t,w)}=\sum_i\eta_i^2\le\eta_1=(1+s(t,w))^{-1}$. In particular $p\ge0$. Rotation interchanges the two periods; substitution in the definitions proves $$\begin{aligned}
 \Delta(w)&=2p(w,w)+p(w,2w),\\
 p(t,2w)&=2p(t,w)-2p(w,t)+p(w,2t),\\
 0\le p(t,w)&\le2s(t,w),\\
 s(t,w)&\le e^{p(t,w)}-1.
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:rectangle-identities}$$ Also, $$e^{-tE(w)}\le s(t,w)
 \le s(t_0,w)e^{-(t-t_0)E(w)}\quad(t\ge t_0).
 \label{eq:wilson-trace-advance}$$ If $p(t,w)\le1/4$, then $s\le pe^p$ gives <a id="eq:wilson-squaring"></a>$$e^{-tE(w)}\le2p(t,w),\qquad
 p(2t,w)\le4p(t,w)^2.
 \label{eq:wilson-squaring}$$ For the second inequality use $p(2t,w)\le2s(2t,w)\le2s(t,w)^2\le2p^2e^{2p}$.

<a id="eq:wilson-basic-tails"></a>
We include the dyadic argument from (**SharpO4?**, Proposition 2.2). If $\Delta(r)\le2^{-10}$, then $p(r,2r)\le\Delta(r)$ and $p(2r,2r)\le4\Delta(r)^2$. The rectangle identity gives $$p(r,4r)\le2p(r,2r)+p(2r,2r)\le3\Delta(r).$$ Squaring yields $p(2r,4r)\le36\Delta(r)^2$, hence $$\Delta(2r)\le44\Delta(r)^2\le64\Delta(r)^2.$$ All squaring steps are justified by $3\cdot2^{-10}<1/4$. Starting with <a href="#eq:wilson-seed" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-seed">[eq:wilson-seed]</a>, this proves on dyadic $w=2^kM_0$, with uniform $c,C>0$, $$\Delta(w)\le Ce^{-cw},\qquad E(w)\ge c,\qquad
 s(w/2,w)\le Ce^{-cw}\quad(w\ge2M_0).
 \label{eq:wilson-basic-tails}$$ Indeed $e^{-wE(w)}\le2p(w,w)\le\Delta(w)$, and $p(w/2,w)\le\Delta(w/2)$ controls the half-time trace.

<a id="stmt-lem-wilson-long-rectangles"></a>
<div id="lem:wilson-long-rectangles" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:wilson-long-rectangle"></a>
**Lemma 9** (Long rectangles). *Uniformly over admitted trajectories with $N\ge N_0$ and $h\in I_H$, for all sufficiently large dyadic $t$ and dyadic $w\ge2t$, $$p(t,w)\le C(w/t)e^{-ct}.
 \label{eq:wilson-long-rectangle}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-wilson-long-rectangles"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-wilson-long-rectangles</summary>

*Proof.* At $w=2t$, $p(t,2t)\le\Delta(t)$. For widths $z=t,2t$, advance the half-circumference estimate <a href="#eq:wilson-basic-tails" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-basic-tails">[eq:wilson-basic-tails]</a> to time $w$ using <a href="#eq:wilson-trace-advance" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-trace-advance">[eq:wilson-trace-advance]</a> and $E(z)\ge c$. This gives $p(w,t)+p(w,2t)\le Ce^{-cw}$, after decreasing $c$. The rectangle identity therefore gives $p(t,2w)\le2p(t,w)+Ce^{-cw}$. Iteration over dyadic widths proves the result. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-14"></a>
#### Convergence of a truncated cylinder rate

Choose dyadic $t\asymp w^{1/2}$ and $t_0\asymp w^{1/4}$, with fixed implicit constants. At widths $W=w,2w$, Lemma <a href="#lem:wilson-long-rectangles" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:wilson-long-rectangles">9</a> makes $s(t_0,W)\le1$ uniformly for all large $w$. Hence <a id="eq:wilson-short-time-sandwich"></a>$$e^{-tE(W)}\le s(t,W)\le e^{-(t-t_0)E(W)},\qquad
 \tfrac12s(t,W)\le p(t,W)\le2s(t,W).
 \label{eq:wilson-short-time-sandwich}$$ The lower bound uses $p\ge\log(1+s)\ge s/2$ when $s\le1$.

We do not yet have a uniform upper bound for $E(W)$. For fixed $B>0$, set $$f_B(t,W)=-\frac1t\log\bigl(p(t,W)+e^{-Bt}\bigr).$$ The preceding sandwich proves <a id="eq:wilson-capped-rate"></a>$$f_B(t,W)=\min\{E(W),B\}+O_B(w^{-1/4}).
 \label{eq:wilson-capped-rate}$$ Its upper and lower exponential rates are $\min\{E(W),B\}$ and $\min\{(1-t_0/t)E(W),B\}$, up to $O(1/t)$. Their difference is at most $Bt_0/t$, even if $E(W)>B$.

The swapped terms in the rectangle identity are $O(e^{-cw})$, so $p(t,2w)=2p(t,w)+O(e^{-cw})$. The added $e^{-Bt}$ bounds both logarithm arguments below, and $t\asymp\sqrt w$ makes the additive error negligible. The factor two changes their logarithms by at most a constant. Thus $|f_B(t,2w)-f_B(t,w)|\le C_B/t$, and $$|\min\{E(2w),B\}-\min\{E(w),B\}|\le C_Bw^{-1/4}.$$ This is summable along dyadic doublings. The truncated rate has a limit for each trajectory, with convergence error $O_B(w^{-1/4})$ uniform over all trajectories.

<a id="pm-h-15"></a>
#### Identification with the plane gap

<a id="eq:wilson-first-gap-direction"></a>
For each fixed trajectory we first prove $$m(\beta)/a\ge\limsup_{w\to\infty}E(w),
 \label{eq:wilson-first-gap-direction}$$ with dyadic widths. If $F$ is a bounded continuous observable in a time slab of $r$ lattice steps, its normalized transfer insertion $A_F$ has norm at most $\|F\|_\infty$. For $r=0$ it is multiplication by $F$; for $r\ge1$ its kernel is pointwise dominated in modulus by $\|F\|_\infty U(w)^r$. For two such insertions, let $d$ be the number of lattice steps from the last row of the first slab to the first row of the second. Then $$|\operatorname{Cov}_{\omega_{\beta,w/a}}(F,G)|
 \le\|F\|_\infty\|G\|_\infty e^{-adE(w)}.$$ The square-torus expectation of $F$ is $$\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(A_F U(w)^{\,w/a-r})}
      {\operatorname{Tr}U(w)^{\,w/a}}.$$ When $ar\le w/2$, separating the ground projection in numerator and denominator bounds its difference from the cylinder expectation by $2\|F\|_\infty s(w/2,w)$. By <a href="#eq:wilson-basic-tails" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-basic-tails">[eq:wilson-basic-tails]</a>, cylinders and square tori therefore have the same local limits, namely the unique periodic plane state.

Take a subsequence realizing the limsup of $E(w)$ and pass the slab inequality to the plane. Applied to reflected local autocorrelations, positivity of their spectral measures and density in the OS space prove <a href="#eq:wilson-first-gap-direction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-first-gap-direction">[eq:wilson-first-gap-direction]</a>. An infinite limsup would give an infinite gap by the same argument, contradicting <a href="#eq:wilson-input-upper" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-input-upper">[eq:wilson-input-upper]</a>.

<a id="eq:wilson-cylinder-limit"></a>
Take $B=10$ in the truncated-rate convergence. Its limit is at most $\log8<10$, by <a href="#eq:wilson-first-gap-direction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-first-gap-direction">[eq:wilson-first-gap-direction]</a> and <a href="#eq:wilson-input-upper" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-input-upper">[eq:wilson-input-upper]</a>. Uniform convergence makes the truncation inactive for all sufficiently large widths, uniformly over the trajectories. Thus $$E_\infty=\lim_{w\to\infty}E(w),\qquad
 |E(w)-E_\infty|\le C_Hw^{-1/4},\qquad
 E_\infty\le m(\beta)/a\le\log8.
 \label{eq:wilson-cylinder-limit}$$

<a id="eq:wilson-visible-pair"></a>
For the reverse inequality, fix $\beta,a$ and keep $t\asymp\sqrt w$. Apply Lemmas <a href="#lem:wilson-detector" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:wilson-detector">5</a> and <a href="#lem:wilson-visibility" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:wilson-visibility">6</a> at $n=t/a$. Since $E(w)$ is bounded, $\tau_{\beta,w/a}=e^{-aE(w)}$ and the detector overlap are bounded below by positive constants for this fixed trajectory. Some pair on the two rows therefore has correlation $$\omega_{\beta,w/a}(q_x^1q_y^1)
 \ge c_\beta'(w/a)^{-2}e^{-tE(w)}.
 \label{eq:wilson-visible-pair}$$ The positive constant is independent of $w$.

<a id="eq:wilson-pair-to-plane"></a>
Lift the spatial pair along a shortest circle arc. Its spatial span is at most $w/2$, and its temporal span $t$ is also at most $w/2$ for large $w$. The cylinder expectation and its plane counterpart satisfy $$\left|\omega_{\beta,w/a}(q_x^1q_y^1)
       -\mathbb E_{\mu_\beta}(q_{\widetilde x}^1
                             q_{\widetilde y}^1)\right|
 \le Ce^{-cw},
 \label{eq:wilson-pair-to-plane}$$ as follows. First compare the cylinder to the $w$ by $w$ torus by the slab estimate, with error at most $2s(w/2,w)$. Compare the $w$ by $w$ and $2w$ by $w$ tori through their common width-$w$ cylinder. Next rotate and compare the $2w$ by $w$ and $2w$ by $2w$ tori through the width-$2w$ cylinder. The latter error is bounded by a constant times $s(w/2,2w)=O(e^{-cw})$, using Lemma <a href="#lem:wilson-long-rectangles" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:wilson-long-rectangles">9</a>. Translations fit the product into the required arcs at every comparison. Repeat these two-direction doublings. Their errors sum to $Ce^{-cw}$. For each initial $w$, the lifted observable is fixed throughout the larger-torus limit, so periodic local convergence proves <a href="#eq:wilson-pair-to-plane" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-pair-to-plane">[eq:wilson-pair-to-plane]</a>.

Because $t\asymp\sqrt w$ and $E(w)$ is bounded, this error is negligible relative to the right side of <a href="#eq:wilson-visible-pair" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-visible-pair">[eq:wilson-visible-pair]</a> as $w\to\infty$ at the fixed trajectory. The plane component pair is at most $e^{-m(\beta)t/a}$ by Proposition <a href="#prop:wilson-full-gap" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:wilson-full-gap">4</a>, regardless of its spatial separation. Taking logarithms gives $$m(\beta)/a
 \le E(w)+\frac{2\log(w/a)-\log(c_\beta'/2)}{t}.$$ The extra term tends to zero, so $m(\beta)/a\le E_\infty$. Together with <a href="#eq:wilson-cylinder-limit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-cylinder-limit">[eq:wilson-cylinder-limit]</a>, this proves equality and <a href="#eq:wilson-cylinder-rate" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-cylinder-rate">[eq:wilson-cylinder-rate]</a>. The fixed-trajectory argument removed the nonuniform visibility constants; the convergence rate was already uniform.

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-wilson-long-rectangles-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-wilson-long-rectangles</summary>

*Completion of Proposition <a href="#prop:cylinder-rate" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:cylinder-rate">[prop:cylinder-rate]</a>.* Apply <a href="#eq:wilson-trace-advance" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wilson-trace-advance">[eq:wilson-trace-advance]</a> at time $w$, with $t_0\asymp w^{1/4}$ and widths $W=w,2w$. The long-rectangle bound gives $s(t_0,W)\le1$, and hence $$e^{-wE(W)}\le s(w,W)\le e^{-(w-t_0)E(W)}.$$ Now $E(W)$ is uniformly bounded and $p(w,W)$ lies between $s(w,W)/2$ and $2s(w,W)$. Therefore $$-w^{-1}\log p(w,W)
 =E(W)+O_H(w^{-3/4})
 =m(\beta)/a+O_H(w^{-1/4}).$$ The positive sum $\Delta(w)=2p(w,w)+p(w,2w)$ has the same logarithmic rate within this error. This proves <a href="#eq:partition-rate" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:partition-rate">[eq:partition-rate]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:brownian"></a>
### The Brownian regulator and its transfer operators

The partition comparison used later introduces a model with continuous space and discrete time. We first construct its transfer operators and identify the state on which their norms can be calculated. The circumference remains finite throughout. This point is essential: the comparison with the lattice model will require a quantitative statement on a specified, growing family of circles.

<a id="pm-h-17"></a>
#### The row measure and particle expansion

Let space be the circle $\mathbb R/W\mathbb Z$, where $W>0$, and let one unit of discrete time be a vertical lattice step. The spin manifold is $$\mathcal G=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z\times SU(2))/
       \bigl((v,Q)\sim(v+\pi,-Q)\bigr),
 \qquad G=e^{iv}Q.$$ We identify $SU(2)$ with the unit sphere $S^3$. On a row, use the unnormalized Brownian loop measure with Hamiltonian $$E=\frac12\bigl(-\partial_v^2-\Delta_{S^3}\bigr),$$ with Haar probability as reference measure. Thus the mass of the row measure is $\operatorname{Tr}e^{-WE}$. We denote integration with respect to this measure by $\mathcal E_W$. For $b>0$, set $\lambda=b^2/2$ and assign successive rows the oriented interaction $$\exp\left\{\lambda\int_0^W
                \operatorname{Tr}\bigl(G_t(x)G_{t+1}(x)^*\bigr)\,dx\right\}.$$ Reversing the orientation complex-conjugates the interaction and gives the same construction after reversing the notation for successive rows.

We use $n_{\mathrm p}$ exclusively for particle number, reserving $N$ for the renormalization depth later in the paper. Expand each vertical exponential. A constant circle rotation on one row multiplies its incoming and outgoing terms by opposite circle characters. Integration over that rotation therefore forces the same particle number on every time-link. A color $A_i=(a_i^L,a_i^R)\in\{1,2\}^2$ records the two matrix indices of the $i$th insertion. The particle Hilbert space is the bosonic subspace of $$L^2\bigl((\mathbb R/W\mathbb Z)^{n_{\mathrm p}};
                     (\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes n_{\mathrm p}}\bigr).$$ Equivalently, we integrate positions over the ordered chamber $0<X_1<\cdots<X_{n_{\mathrm p}}<W$, with the color identifications induced by simultaneous permutation of particles. All kernels below act by integration over this chamber and summation over colors. The chamber integral therefore absorbs the factorial in the exponential series.

<a id="eq:brownian-transfer"></a>
For position and color lists $(X,A)$ and $(Y,B)$, define $$T_{n_{\mathrm p}}(Y,B;X,A)
 =\lambda^{n_{\mathrm p}}\mathcal E_W\left[
       \prod_{i=1}^{n_{\mathrm p}}G_{B_i}(Y_i)
                        \overline{G_{A_i}(X_i)}\right].
 \label{eq:brownian-transfer}$$ For time period $n$, the periodic partition function is $$Z^B_+(n,W)=\sum_{n_{\mathrm p}\ge0}
                   \operatorname{Tr}T_{n_{\mathrm p}}^{\,n}.$$ A minus-center seam in time multiplies each term by $(-1)^{n_{\mathrm p}}$. The expansion is absolutely convergent at every finite period. Each $T_{n_{\mathrm p}}$ is a positive operator: its kernel is the Gram kernel of the insertion functions in the row loop measure. Moreover, $$\sum_{n_{\mathrm p}\ge0}\operatorname{Tr}T_{n_{\mathrm p}}
 =e^{2\lambda W}\operatorname{Tr}e^{-WE}<\infty,$$ because $\sum_{a,b}|G_{ab}|^2=2$. In particular, for each parity $\ell\in\{0,1\}$ the maximum $$\tau_\ell=\max_{n_{\mathrm p}\equiv\ell\ ({\rm mod}\ 2)}
                              \|T_{n_{\mathrm p}}\|$$ is attained.

<a id="stmt-prop-brownian-parity"></a>
<div id="prop:brownian-parity" class="proposition">

<a id="eq:B1"></a>
**Proposition 10** (The parity norm difference). *Let $b\to\infty$, and suppose that for a fixed $D>0$ $$W\asymp e^{\pi b}b^{-1/2}(\log b)^D.$$ Suppose also that there is a fixed $C_*>0$ such that every particle number attaining either parity maximum satisfies $|n_{\mathrm p}/W-b^2|\le C_*b$. Then $$\log\tau_0-\log\tau_1
       \sim32\sqrt2\,b^{1/2}e^{-\pi b}.
 \label{eq:B1}$$*

</div>
